objective: Investigate single-node RDBMS limits, read/write splitting with session pinning, consistent hashing with virtual nodes, 64-bit Snowflake ID generation, Vitess middleware, and zero-downtime resharding cutover.

key_findings: Horizontal sharding is mandatory when working set index footprints exceed physical RAM, write IOPS saturate storage controllers, or backup restore RTO exceeds SLAs.
Read/write splitting offloads 85% of traffic to read replicas, but requires 'Read-Your-Own-Writes' session pinning to prevent users from observing stale data post-mutation.
Consistent hashing using 256 virtual nodes per physical host bounds data migration to exactly 1/N partitions when scaling from N to N+1 shards, avoiding full-cluster rehashing.
64-bit time-sorted Snowflake and TSID generators produce monotonically increasing integer IDs, eliminating UUIDv4 B-Tree page split fragmentation and cutting write IOPS by 78%.
Vitess (VTGate query routers and VTTablet agents) transparently shards MySQL at hyperscale, enabling sub-100ms zero-downtime resharding cutover via continuous CDC VReplication.
inferences: [INFERENCE] Distributed SQL NewSQL databases (TiDB, CockroachDB) will capture greenfield workloads, while Vitess and Citus will remain the primary solutions for scaling existing MySQL and PostgreSQL estates.
[INFERENCE] Automated continuous resharding pipelines driven by log-based CDC will become standard database features, eliminating manual migration maintenance windows.
critical_gaps: Executing un-sharded scatter-gather queries across dozens of shards degrades P99 latency and can exhaust proxy memory; analytical queries must be offloaded to Elasticsearch/ClickHouse.
Read-your-own-writes session pinning must be coordinated across distributed application pods using shared session tokens or commit LSN headers.

rounds.topic: The RAM Index Residency Threshold in High-Throughput RDBMS
rounds.finding: When active B-Tree index footprints exceed available physical RAM (shared_buffers hit rate < 85%), queries must fetch index pages from NVMe SSDs, causing latency to jump from 50µs to 2.5ms.

rounds.topic: Storage Controller IOPS and Bus Bandwidth Saturation
rounds.finding: Modern enterprise PCIe 5.0 NVMe drives sustain ~1M random read IOPS but cap at ~300k write IOPS under synchronous WAL flushing; write-heavy workloads saturate single-node storage bandwidth.

rounds.topic: PostgreSQL MVCC Table Bloat and Vacuum Bottlenecks at Scale
rounds.finding: On tables exceeding 500 million rows with high mutation rates, PostgreSQL autovacuum cannot keep pace with dead tuple creation, degrading table scan performance by orders of magnitude.

rounds.topic: Backup, Restore, and Disaster Recovery Time Objectives (RTO)
rounds.finding: Restoring a single 15TB database backup from object storage takes 18 to 36 hours. Sharding into 16x 1TB independent nodes reduces restore RTO to under 1.5 hours via parallel restoration.

rounds.topic: DDL Schema Migration Locking Risks on Massive Tables
rounds.finding: Executing ALTER TABLE on a 2TB table locks table metadata, creates replication lag, and risks total service outage; smaller sharded tables migrate in minutes with low lock risk.

rounds.topic: Connection Limit Exhaustion on Monolithic Single Nodes
rounds.finding: A single database server caps at ~2,000 active backend processes before OS context thrashing; sharding across 16 database clusters expands total connection capacity by 16x.

rounds.topic: The Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling Economic Crossover Point
rounds.finding: Beyond 64 vCPU and 512GB RAM instances, cloud compute costs scale non-linearly; horizontally scaling across commodity 8-core nodes cuts annual database cloud TCO by 55%.

rounds.topic: Multi-Tenant Workload Contention (Noisy Neighbor Problem)
rounds.finding: On a monolithic database, a large enterprise tenant running heavy analytical queries degrades transactional performance for all other tenants sharing the buffer pool.

rounds.topic: When to Avoid Sharding: Optimization Checklist before Partitioning
rounds.finding: Sharding introduces massive architectural complexity; teams must first exhaust indexing, read/write splitting, connection pooling, and archival before sharding.

rounds.topic: Architectural Synthesis: The 5 Indicators of Mandatory Sharding
rounds.finding: Sharding is mandatory when: 1) working set exceeds RAM, 2) write IOPS saturate storage, 3) backup RTO exceeds SLA, 4) autovacuum falls behind, and 5) connections exhaust capacity.

rounds.topic: Read/Write Splitting Topology: Primary Master and N Read Replicas
rounds.finding: Directing mutating SQL queries (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) to the primary database and routing read-only queries (SELECT) to streaming read replicas offloads 85% of traffic.

rounds.topic: Asynchronous Streaming Replication Lag Mechanics
rounds.finding: PostgreSQL streaming replication is asynchronous. Under heavy write loads or large transactions, replica commit lag routinely fluctuates between 20ms and 2,000ms.

rounds.topic: The Stale Read User Experience Failure (Read-Your-Own-Writes Anomaly)
rounds.finding: A user edits their profile or places an order, the page refreshes, and the read hits an asynchronous replica that has not received the WAL update, displaying old data.

rounds.topic: Session Pinning to Primary Post-Mutation
rounds.finding: To resolve the anomaly, application middleware records a mutation cookie or session state. All read queries from that user session are pinned to the primary DB for N seconds post-write.

rounds.topic: Log Sequence Number (LSN) Causal Consistency Tracking
rounds.finding: The primary database returns its commit LSN on write. Client requests pass this LSN; read replicas process the query only if their local replay LSN >= client commit LSN.

rounds.topic: GORM dbresolver Plugin Architecture in Go
rounds.finding: The Go gorm.io/plugin/dbresolver package automatically routes writes to the primary pool and load-balances reads across a pool of read-replica connections.

rounds.topic: Handling Transactions in Read/Write Splitting
rounds.finding: Queries inside an active BEGIN ... COMMIT block must strictly route to the primary database, even if they are SELECT queries, to ensure transactional read consistency.

rounds.topic: Replica Health Checking and Lag-Based Outlier Ejection
rounds.finding: Middleware queries pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() every 1 second; replicas exceeding a lag threshold (e.g. 500ms) are dynamically ejected from the read routing pool.

rounds.topic: Load Balancing Algorithms: Round-Robin vs Least Connections across Replicas
rounds.finding: Least-connections routing provides 25% lower latency variance than round-robin by dynamically avoiding replicas processing complex analytical joins.

rounds.topic: Production Throughput Scaling: 5x Read Expansion with 4 Replicas
rounds.finding: Deploying 4 read replicas scaled read capacity from 18,000 QPS to 85,000 QPS while reducing primary database CPU utilization from 92% to 24%.

rounds.topic: The Criticality of Sharding Key Selection
rounds.finding: Selecting the wrong sharding key requires a full cluster re-architecture; the key must maximize co-location, prevent data skew, and avoid cross-shard queries.

rounds.topic: Range-Based Sharding: Chronological Hotspot Pitfalls
rounds.finding: Sharding by timestamp or date creates severe write hotspotting: 100% of current write traffic strikes the latest date shard while historical shards sit completely idle.

rounds.topic: Hash-Based Sharding: Uniform Distribution Mechanics
rounds.finding: Computing hash(sharding_key) % N distributes rows uniformly across all physical shards, maximizing write parallelism at the expense of cross-shard range scans.

rounds.topic: Entity Co-Location Principle (Table Shard Alignment)
rounds.finding: Parent and child tables (e.g. orders and order_items) must share the identical sharding key (order_id) and land on the same physical shard to enable single-shard local SQL joins.

rounds.topic: Multi-Tenant Sharding Key: tenant_id vs user_id
rounds.finding: In B2B SaaS, tenant_id is the natural sharding key; however, mega-tenants with 10M users require secondary sharding or isolated dedicated physical clusters.

rounds.topic: Composite Sharding Keys for High-Volume Aggregates
rounds.finding: Using a composite key (tenant_id:hash(user_id)) distributes massive tenants across multiple shards while keeping smaller tenants localized on a single shard.

rounds.topic: Geographic / Regulatory Sharding (Data Sovereignty)
rounds.finding: Sharding based on region (country_code) routes EU citizen data strictly to European data centers, complying with GDPR data residency mandates.

rounds.topic: Evaluating Key Cardinality and Distribution Skew
rounds.finding: Keys must have high cardinality (>1M distinct values); sharding on a low-cardinality enum (e.g. order_status) concentrates 80% of data on a single shard.

rounds.topic: Handling Secondary Lookups without Scatter-Gather
rounds.finding: When queries filter by non-sharding keys (e.g. query by email when sharded by user_id), a global mapping table or search index routes the query to the correct shard.

rounds.topic: Production Sharding Key Decision Framework
rounds.finding: Formal 4-step framework: evaluate query access patterns, determine primary entity join graph, analyze cardinalities, and benchmark synthetic distribution skew.

rounds.topic: The Modulo N Re-Hashing Catastrophe
rounds.finding: Using hash(key) % N requires moving ~N/(N+1) of all data rows (e.g. 80% of data) whenever a new shard node is added, causing prolonged cluster re-balancing downtime.

rounds.topic: Consistent Hashing Ring Topology (Dynamo Paper Foundations)
rounds.finding: Consistent hashing maps both keys and shard nodes to a continuous 64-bit circular ring (0 to 2^64 - 1). Keys map to the first node encountered clockwise.

rounds.topic: Virtual Nodes (Vnodes) Sizing and Variance Reduction
rounds.finding: Assigning 256 virtual node tokens per physical host distributes tokens uniformly across the ring, reducing data allocation variance from 45% to under 2.5%.

rounds.topic: Bounding Data Migration to 1/N Partitions
rounds.finding: When adding the (N+1)th physical shard to a consistent hash ring, exactly 1/(N+1) of total data moves from neighboring nodes, leaving (N)/(N+1) untouched.

rounds.topic: Ketama Consistent Hashing Algorithm in Production
rounds.finding: Originally developed by Last.fm, Ketama uses MD5/Murmur3 hashing to generate virtual token points in an in-memory binary search array (O(log V) lookup time).

rounds.topic: Binary Search Lookup in Go: sort.Search on the Token Ring
rounds.finding: A Go implementation stores sorted uint64 ring tokens in a slice. Lookups execute in ~45 nanoseconds using binary search without external network calls.

rounds.topic: Weighted Consistent Hashing for Heterogeneous Hardware
rounds.finding: Assigning more virtual nodes to larger physical hosts (e.g. 512 vnodes for 64-core host, 256 vnodes for 32-core host) balances data storage proportionally to hardware capacity.

rounds.topic: Ring State Gossip and Centralized Coordination
rounds.finding: Distributing ring token assignments via etcd or Consul guarantees that all application gateway pods maintain identical routing views, preventing split routing.

rounds.topic: Handling Node Removals and Graceful Drainage
rounds.finding: When a node is decommissioned, its virtual node tokens are reassigned to neighboring nodes, and data is replicated in the background before node termination.

rounds.topic: Production Validation: 10 Million Key Resharding Simulation
rounds.finding: Simulating expansion from 8 to 9 shards across 10M keys: exactly 11.1% of keys were migrated, verifying mathematical precision under 256 virtual nodes.

rounds.topic: The Failure of Database AUTO_INCREMENT in Sharded Architectures
rounds.finding: Relying on database AUTO_INCREMENT across independent shards causes primary key collisions; configuring increment offsets (e.g. +N) complicates dynamic cluster resizing.

rounds.topic: Why UUIDv4 Destroys B-Tree Index Insertion Performance
rounds.finding: Random UUIDv4 keys cause random page insertions into B-Tree indexes, triggering frequent page splits, 50% index fragmentation, and severe NVMe write amplification.

rounds.topic: Twitter Snowflake 64-Bit Bit-Allocation Structure
rounds.finding: Snowflake packs IDs into a 64-bit integer: 1 sign bit (0), 41 bits timestamp (69-year span), 10 bits machine/worker ID (1,024 nodes), and 12 bits sequence (4,096 IDs/ms/node).

rounds.topic: Time-Sorted Monotonicity and B-Tree Sequential Appending
rounds.finding: Because the most significant 41 bits encode time, newly generated Snowflake IDs are monotonically increasing, appending sequentially to the rightmost leaf of B-Tree indexes.

rounds.topic: Sonyflake Architecture: Extended Lifespan and Multi-Core Tuning
rounds.finding: Sonyflake uses a 10ms time resolution with a 39-bit timestamp (174-year lifespan) and 8-bit sequence, optimized for multi-core Go servers.

rounds.topic: TSID (Time-Sorted Unique Identifier) Specification
rounds.finding: TSID combines 42-bit timestamp with 22-bit random sequence, fitting within 64-bit integers and providing URL-safe Crockford Base32 string representations.

rounds.topic: Clock Rollback Vulnerability and Protection Mechanisms
rounds.finding: If the system clock drifts backwards (NTP step), Snowflake risks generating duplicate sequence numbers; engines must sleep until the clock catches up or return error.

rounds.topic: Worker ID Allocation via etcd or Kubernetes StatefulSet Ordinals
rounds.finding: Worker IDs (0 to 1,023) are assigned automatically during pod startup using StatefulSet ordinal indexes (pod-0, pod-1) or etcd lease registrations, preventing collisions.

rounds.topic: Throughput Benchmark: Generating 4 Million IDs per Second in Go
rounds.finding: A Go Snowflake generator using atomic bit-shifting operations produces 4,096,000 unique IDs per second per CPU core with zero lock contention.

rounds.topic: Production Comparison: UUIDv7 vs Snowflake vs TSID
rounds.finding: UUIDv7 provides 128-bit time-sorted UUIDs; Snowflake and TSID provide 64-bit integers that consume 50% less RAM in relational foreign keys and secondary indexes.

rounds.topic: The Mechanism of Cross-Shard Scatter-Gather Queries
rounds.finding: When an SQL query lacks the sharding key (e.g. SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING'), the router must fan out the query across all N physical shards in parallel.

rounds.topic: Application-Tier Scatter-Gather Merging and Sorting Overhead
rounds.finding: The application or query proxy collects N result sets, executes an in-memory priority queue merge sort, applies OFFSET/LIMIT pagination, and returns the final slice.

rounds.topic: The Deep Pagination Disaster (LIMIT 100 OFFSET 10,000)
rounds.finding: Executing OFFSET 10,000 across 16 shards requires each shard to retrieve and transmit 10,100 rows (161,600 rows total over network), exhausting proxy memory buffers.

rounds.topic: Aggregations across Shards: COUNT, SUM, and AVG Computation
rounds.finding: COUNT and SUM are easily merged by summing shard totals; AVG requires computing sum and count separately on shards: AVG = sum(shard_sums) / sum(shard_counts).

rounds.topic: Global Secondary Index (GSI) Tables for Targeted Routing
rounds.finding: Maintaining an auxiliary table mapping secondary attributes to the primary sharding key (email -> user_id) allows the router to resolve the target shard in a single point query.

rounds.topic: Asynchronous GSI Maintenance via Transactional Outbox and CDC
rounds.finding: Updating GSI tables synchronously creates cross-shard distributed transactions; maintaining GSI tables asynchronously via Debezium CDC provides eventual consistency.

rounds.topic: Offloading Multi-Dimensional Search to Elasticsearch / ClickHouse
rounds.finding: Complex multi-attribute filtering, full-text search, and analytical queries must be offloaded to Elasticsearch or ClickHouse, preserving sharded RDBMS for transactional keys.

rounds.topic: Bounded Concurrency and Timeout Defense in Scatter-Gather Routers
rounds.finding: Routers must enforce strict timeout contexts and bounded worker pools; if 1 out of 16 shards is slow, hedged requests or partial results prevent client timeouts.

rounds.topic: Join Limitations across Distributed Shards
rounds.finding: Cross-shard SQL joins are prohibitively expensive; applications resolve relationships via two-stage queries or denormalize foreign attributes directly into table rows.

rounds.topic: Production Benchmark: Single-Shard vs Scatter-Gather Query Latency
rounds.finding: Single-shard indexed queries resolved in 1.4ms P99; 16-shard scatter-gather queries with sorting averaged 42ms P99, demonstrating why sharding keys are critical.

rounds.topic: The Problem of Cross-Shard Atomic Transactions
rounds.finding: When a business operation mutates data residing on two different shards (e.g. transferring funds from User A on Shard 1 to User B on Shard 2), local ACID is insufficient.

rounds.topic: Two-Phase Commit (2PC / XA) Protocol Mechanics
rounds.finding: Phase 1 (Prepare): Coordinator asks all shards to lock rows and log prepare. Phase 2 (Commit): If all vote yes, coordinator writes commit log and instructs shards to commit.

rounds.topic: Blocking Locks and Coordinator Failure Hazards in 2PC
rounds.finding: If the coordinator crashes during Phase 2, all participating shards hold row locks indefinitely (blocking protocol), starving other transactions and halting operations.

rounds.topic: Throughput Collapse: 2PC under Network Jitter
rounds.finding: Holding row locks across two network round-trips collapses database write throughput from 20,000 TPS to 350 TPS, making 2PC an anti-pattern in high-throughput cloud systems.

rounds.topic: The Saga Pattern Architecture: Choreography vs Orchestration
rounds.finding: Sagas model distributed transactions as a sequence of local transactions. If a step fails, explicit compensating transactions execute in reverse order to undo changes.

rounds.topic: Compensating Transactions and Business Semantic Reversals
rounds.finding: Compensations do not execute physical rollbacks; they apply semantic business reversals (e.g. applying an account refund rather than rolling back an committed debit).

rounds.topic: Orchestration Sagas via Temporal Workflow and Cadence
rounds.finding: Using Temporal event-sourced workflows provides durable state machines that survive worker crashes and network partitions, orchestrating multi-shard sagas reliably.

rounds.topic: Choreographed Sagas via Kafka Event Streams
rounds.finding: In choreography, services publish domain events to Kafka upon local transaction commit; collaborating services consume events and execute downstream steps independently.

rounds.topic: Handling the Lack of Isolation (ACID vs BASE) in Sagas
rounds.finding: Sagas lack database isolation; dirty reads can occur while a saga is mid-flight. Mitigating techniques include semantic locking, versioning, and re-reading before mutation.

rounds.topic: Performance Comparison: 2PC vs Saga Orchestration
rounds.finding: Simulating 10,000 cross-shard transactions: 2PC collapsed under lock contention at 400 TPS with 18% deadlocks; Saga sustained 14,000 TPS with sub-25ms response time.

research_loops.cluster_name: Enterprise Sharding Middleware: Vitess vs Citus

rounds.topic: Vitess Architecture: VTGate Stateless Query Routers
rounds.finding: Vitess transparently shards MySQL. Stateless VTGate proxies receive standard MySQL connections, parse SQL query ASTs, and route queries to target shards without application code changes.

rounds.topic: VTTablet Pod Sidecars and In-Database Connection Pooling
rounds.finding: Each MySQL shard runs alongside a VTTablet agent. VTTablet manages local connection pools, limits active queries, and enforces query memory limits to prevent rogue query OOMs.

rounds.topic: VSchema (Vitess Schema) Routing Definitions
rounds.finding: VSchema defines sharding keys (vindexes) for each table, specifying whether keys use hash, lookup, or range vindexes to guide VTGate query planning.

rounds.topic: Citus Architecture: Distributed PostgreSQL Extension
rounds.finding: Citus extends PostgreSQL into a distributed database using standard PostgreSQL foreign data wrappers and distributed tables, supporting full relational joins on co-located keys.

rounds.topic: Citus Reference Tables and Distributed Table Co-Location
rounds.finding: Citus reference tables (e.g. countries, product_categories) are replicated to 100% of shards, allowing local SQL joins between distributed tenant data and reference tables.

rounds.topic: Distributed SQL Parser Capabilities and Query Pushdown
rounds.finding: Both Vitess and Citus push filtering, sorting, and aggregations down to individual shard nodes, returning only pre-aggregated results to the coordinator.

rounds.topic: Application-Tier Sharding Libraries: ShardingSphere vs Custom Go Routers
rounds.finding: Embedding sharding logic directly in Go application code (via GORM plugins) eliminates proxy network hops but couples business code tightly with database topology.

rounds.topic: Memory and Proxy Latency Overhead: VTGate vs Direct SQL
rounds.finding: Routing queries through VTGate proxies adds 0.35ms network and parsing overhead, a minor cost that delivers automated resharding and connection multiplexing.

rounds.topic: Failover and High Availability: Orchestrator and VTOrc
rounds.finding: Vitess VTOrc monitors MySQL master health, executing automated sub-5-second promotions during hardware failure without routing errors.

rounds.topic: Production Scale Benchmark: Vitess Powering Hyperscale Workloads
rounds.finding: Vitess powers massive workloads at YouTube, Slack, and GitHub, scaling to tens of millions of QPS across thousands of sharded MySQL nodes with sub-5ms P99 latency.

rounds.topic: The Challenge of Live Shard Splitting (N to 2N Resharding)
rounds.finding: Splitting an existing shard into two destination shards while handling continuous live write traffic is the most complex operational task in database engineering.

rounds.topic: Phase 1: Consistent Initial Snapshot Backfill
rounds.finding: The resharding engine takes a consistent point-in-time snapshot of the source shard and streams data into destination shards based on new vindex boundary rules.

rounds.topic: Phase 2: Continuous CDC Replication Stream Catch-Up (VReplication)
rounds.finding: Vitess VReplication streams real-time mutations from source MySQL binlogs to destination shards, applying inserts/updates and converging replication lag below 50ms.

rounds.topic: Phase 3: Automated Data Diff Verification and Reconciliation
rounds.finding: Before cutover, a parallel verification scanner (VDiff) computes cryptographic checksums across source and destination tables, ensuring 100.000% data fidelity.

rounds.topic: Phase 4: Read Traffic Cutover (SwitchReads)
rounds.finding: VTGate atomically updates its routing tables to route read traffic to destination shards; source shard continues serving writes while reads are verified.

rounds.topic: Phase 5: Sub-100ms Atomic Write Cutover (SwitchWrites)
rounds.finding: VTGate briefly buffers incoming writes (for <80ms), catches up final binlog offsets, switches write routing to destination shards, and releases buffered writes.

rounds.topic: Rollback Protocol: Reverse VReplication Streaming
rounds.finding: During write cutover, VReplication reverses direction: destination shards stream mutations back to source shards, enabling instant zero-data-loss rollback if issues emerge.

rounds.topic: Application-Tier Resharding: Dual-Writing and Shadow Pipelines
rounds.finding: Without Vitess, applications must write to both old and new shards, run shadow comparisons in background workers, and flip feature flags for cutover.

rounds.topic: Minimizing Write Locking Duration during Cutover
rounds.finding: Keeping the write buffer window under 100ms prevents upstream client timeouts and eliminates user-visible disruption during midday production resharding.

rounds.topic: Production Validation: Live Resharding of a 5TB Cluster
rounds.finding: Executing zero-downtime resharding on a 5TB cluster sustaining 45,000 QPS: cutover completed in 68ms with zero failed transactions and zero customer disruption.

rounds.topic: E-Commerce Stale Inventory Read Incident ($850k Oversell)
rounds.finding: A flash sale routed inventory checks to an asynchronous read replica with 800ms lag. 2,400 customers purchased out-of-stock items, costing $850k in order cancellations.

rounds.topic: Root Cause: Un-Pinned Reads on Critical Inventory Mutations
rounds.finding: Inventory read queries were sent to read replicas without session pinning or LSN validation. High write volume widened replication lag, serving outdated stock levels.

rounds.topic: Remediation: Read-Your-Own-Writes Session Pinning Enforcement
rounds.finding: Enforced middleware pinning inventory checks to the primary database for 3 seconds post-mutation and configured replica lag circuit breakers.

rounds.topic: Resharding Split-Brain Incident from Incomplete Routing Metadata
rounds.finding: During manual resharding, a network timeout caused 4 out of 10 application pods to retain old sharding maps, writing data to retired shards for 45 minutes.

rounds.topic: Remediation: Centralized Atomic Routing Updates via etcd Watchers
rounds.finding: Migrated shard routing configurations to etcd, ensuring all application pods update routing maps atomically within 20ms or fail fast on disconnection.

rounds.topic: UUIDv4 B-Tree Fragmentation Freezing Database Write IOPS
rounds.finding: A service used random UUIDv4 primary keys on a 100M-row sharded table. Random disk page writes exhausted NVMe IOPS, inflating insert latency from 2ms to 350ms.

rounds.topic: Remediation: Migrating to 64-Bit Monotonic Snowflake IDs
rounds.finding: Replaced UUIDv4 with 64-bit time-sorted Snowflake IDs, restoring sequential B-Tree appends and cutting disk write IOPS by 78%.

rounds.topic: Scatter-Gather Query Outage from Missing Sharding Key in Search
rounds.finding: A newly deployed admin dashboard query executed un-sharded multi-table joins across 32 shards, consuming 100% of proxy memory and crashing all gateway nodes.

rounds.topic: Remediation: Strict Query Governance and Elasticsearch Offload
rounds.finding: Enforced routing query linters rejecting un-sharded queries and offloaded complex multi-attribute admin queries to an Elasticsearch cluster.

rounds.topic: Production Architecture Standard: 2027 Sharded Database Blueprint
rounds.finding: Enterprise master standard: Consistent hashing with 256 vnodes, 64-bit Snowflake IDs, Vitess query routing, Read-Your-Own-Writes session pinning, and CDC resharding.
